newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Agriculture Dept. changes worry groups.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Agriculture Dept. changes worry groups.

text.p: Two Clinton administration achievements -- modernising meat inspection and school lunches -- may be in peril with the departure of key leaders at the Agriculture Department, consumer groups said Thursday.

With the decision by Ellen Haas to resign as head of federal food programmes, four of the department's six undersecretary slots will be open. The jobs control public-feeding programmes, meat inspection, agricultural research and the multibillion-dollar farm and export aid portfolios.

"I think backsliding is clearly a danger now," said Caroline Smith DeWaal of the consumer group Centre for Science in the Public Interest, which was active on meat inspection and school lunch reform. "We need strong leaders in those positions."

New leaders could soften the new meat inspection programme, which takes effect this month, or provide too much leeway on rules that require healthy school lunches, said DeWaal and Bob Hahn of the consumer group Public Voice for Food and Health Policy.

Republicans on Capitol Hill said the turnover might herald warmer relations with the Agriculture Department. Kansas Senator Pat Roberts, a Republican, said he hoped for a "more policy-oriented" team rather than activists with their own agenda. Haas was a lightning rod for Republican criticism and Michael Taylor, who resigned last autumn as food safety undersecretary, was accused of being a heavy-handed regulator.

Aides to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman said there would be no change in the new meat inspection regime or mandates for school lunches to comply with the Dietary Guidelines, which call for lower-fat meals, by autumn 1998.

Sceptics "are obviously people outside of the department," said Greg Frazier, Glickman's chief of staff. Healthier school lunches "are right on track," he said, and Thomas Billy, head of the meat inspection agency, was "extraordinarily capable."
Billy, well regarded by consumer groups, was filling in as undersecretary for food safety as well. Acting undersecretaries also have been named for research and farm programmes.

Nonetheless, there was concern on Capitol Hill to see permanent office-holders in the posts. Congress must reauthorize agricultural research programmes this year and the job would be easier with an undersecretary in place, said a House Agriculture Committee staff worker.
There has been little sign of action. Few names surfaced as potential nominees. Aides said Glickman was "concentrating on these issues" but set no timeline for an announcement.

A half-dozen men were mentioned for farm programme undersecretary. They were J.B. Penn of Sparks Companies; Dallas Smith, the acting undersecretary; Gus Schumacher, head of the Foreign Agricultural Service; Robert Young, co-director of the Food and Agricultural Policy Research Institute; and Jill Long, now undersecretary for rural development.
Cathy Wotecki, acting undersecretary, was mentioned as a candidate for the job, along with Floyd Horn, head of the Agricultural Research Service.
Billy was the popular among consumer groups as a possible undersecretary for food safety.

Mentioned as possible candidates for nutrition undersecretary were Shirley Watkins, Haas' deputy; Ed Barron, a Senate staff worker; and Rob Fersh of the antihunger group Food Research and Action Centre.
